topComments.author: gopalv

topComments.author: getbrew
topComments.text: The HOT chapter is the one with the most direct practical payoff. Two things worth knowing from it: HOT only kicks in when no indexed column changes and the new tuple fits on the same page, so an index on a frequently-updated column (status, updated_at) quietly disables it for every update to that table. And lowering fillfactor (say 80-90) on update-heavy tables leaves free space on each page so HOT can actually happen. Comparing n_tup_hot_upd to n_tup_upd in pg_stat_user_tables is a cheap way to see whether you're getting HOT updates before tuning anything.

stories.title: The lost malloc()
stories.author: matt_d

topComments.author: paaloeye
topComments.text: Never seen a 4 points story on the front page.

topComments.author: jdw64
topComments.text: When I was a college student (15 years ago), I first encountered C through A Book on C, and C seems like a language that is simple but can really do a lot. Looking at how old this language is, and how many concepts already used in modern languages were tried during its development history, is surprising. It's surprising that the concepts I thought were modern techniques today were already being tried decades ago—that is, before I was even born. It's amazing that a method like the Bump Allocator was already tried. How were the senior programmers able to do all of this? I'm just amazed.

topComments.author: veltas
topComments.text: I don't associate with the author that well here because I'm not hyped about 'arena allocators' and I don't really care that free doesn't receive a size. I think the interface was okay. Also 'arena allocators' (this meant something different like 20 years ago so I think the name just got rebranded) are not that good, they make some things easier and improve performance sometimes, they also are liable to use more memory and cause more fragmentation if not used with care. That is one of the many reasons why we slowly evolved away from the old linear allocators, but also because we just wanted a simple and flexible interface to hide complexity.

topComments.author: OskarS
topComments.text: > Not only that, mfree() receives the size of the object it is deallocating, as it should . I've always thought that one of the biggest tiny mistakes in the history of this industry. It means, more or less, that you're forcing the memory allocator to keep track of these sizes when it shouldn't have to. There's virtually no sensible case where the person calling free() doesn't know the size of the allocation, so now we're keeping that book-keeping twice, in "user-space" and inside the memory allocator. Like, think about the cases when you'd call malloc: * For allocating a single object of type T, the size is just `sizeof(T)`, so you can just pass that to free() * For allocating an array of objects, the size is `count * sizeof(T)`, and I can't think of a single time where you DON'T know what `count` is. It's either statically sized (in which case it's just a constant), or if you have a dynamically growing array, you need to keep track of the reserved space to know when you reallocate. If nothing else, you need it for bounds-checking. * For chunks of raw memory, you also presumably know when deallocating what the size of the raw memory you allocated is, for the same reasons as the previous point. Like, just having a raw char* pointer lying around with no size information is just terrible C practice. If you truly don't know the size of your allocation (very hard to imagine when this would ever happen), you should be forced on the user-side to keep track of it somehow, not delegate that to the allocator. It's a tiny amount of overhead, but it's for EVERY SINGLE MEMORY ALLOCATION since like 1975. Imagine how many times malloc() and free() has called since then! How much electricity, CPU usage, and memory has been wasted! It boggles the mind!
